questions.stem: A five-year council housing repairs contract starts on Monday. The agreed objective is to cut repeat visits for the same fault from 22 per cent of jobs to under 10 per cent, because every return visit costs a resident another day at home. The 60 operatives receive their work through a handheld app showing the address, the fault code and the time allowed. Nothing they see mentions repeat visits. Supervisors brief each crew at the depot every morning. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Add the repeat-visit figure to the daily depot briefing and give each crew its own number every week.
options.rationale: The people whose decisions produce repeat visits currently receive nothing that mentions them. The briefing already reaches those crews daily, so the objective arrives where the work is actually decided.

options.text: Ask the contract manager to write the repeat-visit target into every operative's annual performance review and objectives.
options.rationale: It treats an annual appraisal as a way to shape a decision someone takes forty times a day. The feedback arrives too late and too far from the job to inform any of them.

options.text: Publish the objective, together with the 22 per cent baseline, in the monthly programme newsletter circulated to the council's housing department.
options.rationale: It reaches an audience that is already informed and misses the one that is not. Promoting a purpose to people who cannot act on it feels like communication and changes nothing.

options.text: Wait until the first quarter of repeat-visit data is in before telling the crews what the contract is aiming at, so that the figure they are given is sound.
options.rationale: It withholds an already agreed objective for three months of live work on the grounds of measuring it. The crews spend a quarter unable to aim at a target that was settled before they started.

questions.explanation: A shared purpose only exists where it reaches the people whose routine decisions determine it, through a channel they already use and at the frequency they take those decisions. Publishing it to an audience that cannot act on it, or deferring it until the data is tidy, leaves the work being done by people aiming at something else. Ask who decides the outcome day to day, then ask what they see.
questions.mindset: Put the objective where the work is decided, not where it is reported.

questions.stem: An online pharmacy's team has raised its velocity for six sprints running and opens every review with the trend. The product goal is to reduce the share of patients who run out of medication before their repeat prescription arrives; that figure has sat at 9 per cent since the first release. The last three retrospectives produced throughput actions only. At today's review the delivery manager congratulates the team on the velocity chart. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Keep velocity as the headline of the review and report the 9 per cent alongside it, so both trends stay visible.
options.rationale: Two measures shown together are not two measures weighted equally. Leaving velocity in the headline position keeps it as the definition of a good sprint, and the outcome becomes a footnote nobody is answerable for.

options.text: Open the next review with the 9 per cent, report progress against it, and keep velocity as an internal capacity check.
options.rationale: What a team reports as success becomes what it optimises. Moving the outcome into the position velocity holds resets the question the review asks, while velocity still does honest work as a planning input.

options.text: Run a retrospective into why the outcome has not moved before changing anything about what the review reports.
options.rationale: Diagnosis is sound in general, but this team's last three retrospectives already produced throughput actions. Investigating inside the frame that caused the drift tends to return another answer shaped like the frame.

options.text: Ask the product owner to re-order the backlog so the next sprint takes only items that touch the 9 per cent directly.
options.rationale: It changes what gets built without changing what the team is asked to prove. Once the reordered items ship, success will again be judged by how quickly they shipped.

questions.explanation: A team steers by whatever it is asked to report, so the measure in the headline position is a working statement of what the effort is for. Velocity describes how much capacity a team has; it cannot say whether that capacity is buying anything. Where output is climbing and the outcome is flat, the first thing to change is the question being answered in public, because every other corrective has to travel through it.
questions.mindset: Whatever a team reports as success is the purpose it will actually pursue.

questions.stem: You manage gate automation at a container terminal. Two directors co-signed the charter and both approve the stage gates. In your weekly one-to-one the operations director describes the priority as cutting driver turnaround time; in a separate meeting the finance director describes it as reducing gate staffing cost. Both objectives are in the approved documents and the next design choice serves one at the expense of the other. Neither director has heard the other's version. The decision is due in ten days.

options.text: Design to the operations director's priority, on the grounds that driver turnaround is the measure the terminal is judged on by the shipping lines that use it.
options.rationale: It settles a question of intent by guessing which sponsor matters more. A project manager choosing between two signatories has taken a governance decision they do not hold, and will own the consequences alone.

options.text: Record both objectives in the project documentation, log the tension between them as a risk, and bring it back for review at each stage gate.
options.rationale: Logging a contradiction is not resolving it. A risk entry leaves the design decision ten days away with two incompatible definitions of success still live and nobody assigned to choose.

options.text: Put both directors in one session, state the two objectives as you have heard them, and ask for a ranking before the decision.
options.rationale: The contradiction is invisible to the only people who can settle it, because each has heard only their own version. Stating both in one room converts a private assumption into a decision they are able to take.

options.text: Ask the sponsor's office to arbitrate between the two objectives on the project's behalf, in time for the design review in ten days.
options.rationale: It routes a live disagreement through a third party who was in neither conversation. The two directors receive a verdict rather than owning a trade-off they are much better placed to weigh.

questions.explanation: Contradictory statements of purpose survive because nobody has heard both at once. The project manager's job is neither to choose between sponsors nor to log the conflict, but to make it visible to the people with standing to resolve it, in time for the decision that turns on it. A conflict surfaced before the commitment is a conversation; the same conflict surfaced after the design is fixed is a dispute with a cost attached.
questions.mindset: Where two sponsors disagree about the point of the work, your job is to get the disagreement into one room.

questions.stem: Six months into a materials-recovery facility upgrade, your engineering team argues that the stated objective — raising sorted-plastics throughput by 30 per cent — is the wrong one, because contamination is what actually loses money on every load. They have eighteen months of plant data and they are probably right. The business case, the funding and the stage gates are all written against throughput. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Adopt contamination as the objective the team works to, and let the business case be corrected at the next scheduled revision of the funding papers.
options.rationale: It changes what the project is for on the strength of being right, which is not the same as holding the authority to decide. Two definitions of success then run in parallel, one of them undocumented.

options.text: Take the team's analysis to the sponsor as a proposal to reconsider the objective, with the throughput case still being delivered.
options.rationale: A challenge to the objective is information its owner needs. Raising it while continuing to deliver the agreed case keeps the project honest and leaves the decision with the person who funded it.

options.text: Ask the team to keep working to throughput and put the contamination argument to the next annual portfolio review.
options.rationale: A twelve-month wait spends the remaining budget on an objective the team has evidence against. Deferring a live challenge to a distant forum is a way of declining it without having to say so.

options.text: Have the team quantify what changing the objective would do to the approved benefits, so the sponsor gets a comparison.
options.rationale: A sponsor cannot weigh a change of objective against an approved case unless someone converts the argument into the same units. Turning a technical insight into a benefits comparison is what makes it decidable.

options.text: Add contamination to the project's monthly reporting as a second objective standing alongside the approved throughput target.
options.rationale: Adding an objective changes the business case without the business case being opened. It also hands the team two things to optimise and no stated priority between them when they conflict.

questions.explanation: A team that challenges the objective is doing the project a service, and the response is neither to adopt the challenge nor to bury it. Objectives belong to whoever approved funding against them, so the work is to convert the challenge into the terms that owner decides in, and to keep delivering the agreed case until they have decided. Being right about the objective does not transfer the authority to change it.
questions.mindset: Take a challenge to the purpose to whoever owns the purpose, and keep delivering until they answer.

questions.stem: A museum's digital team plans its sprint and writes the goal as: finish the eight ticketing stories, the two accessibility fixes and the card-reader spike. A developer who joined last week asks what the sprint is for. The product owner answers that the goal is the list and that everything on it matters. The team's product goal is to let a visitor buy and collect a timed ticket without queueing. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Accept the list as the sprint goal, since the product owner is the person accountable for what a sprint contains.
options.rationale: It confuses ownership of the contents with the form the goal takes. A product owner choosing the items does not turn an inventory of items into a statement of intent.

options.text: Ask the team to trim the sprint backlog until the items that remain share an obvious theme that can be named.
options.rationale: Cutting scope until a theme appears works backwards. The goal should be settled first and the items chosen to serve it, rather than discovered by deletion once the work is picked.

options.text: Leave the goal as it stands for this sprint and raise the point at the retrospective, once the team has seen how the fortnight worked out.
options.rationale: A sprint goal exists to guide the decisions taken inside the sprint, so a correction arriving afterwards misses everything the goal was for.

options.text: Ask the product owner what this sprint should let a visitor do that they cannot today, and write that as the goal.
options.rationale: A sprint goal names the outcome the sprint is buying, which is what lets the team trade items off when the fortnight gets tight. Deriving it from the product goal keeps the two connected.

questions.explanation: A goal states what will be true afterwards; a list is an inventory of work. The difference shows up on the day the sprint runs short, because a goal tells the team which items can be dropped without failing, and a list tells them only that they have failed. The same test applies at any level of intent: if it cannot survive the loss of one item, it is not a goal.
questions.mindset: If it cannot tell you what to drop when time runs out, it is a list rather than a goal.

questions.stem: A university is modernising admissions over three years, funded in two tranches, and the delivery team is asked what the programme is for by a different audience every week. Match each question to the statement of intent that is the right instrument for answering it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Why the university is spending £4 million on admissions at all, and what it expects back for it.
What must be demonstrably true by the end of year two for the remaining funding to be released.
What this quarter's release should let an applicant do that they cannot do today.

options.text: The business case
options.rationale: A business case answers why the investment is worth making and what the organisation expects in return. It is the only instrument here that has to justify not doing the programme at all.

options.text: The dated year-two outcome target
options.rationale: A dated outcome target is what a funding decision can be taken against. It converts the case into something that can be found true or false at a fixed point in the calendar.

options.text: The release goal
options.rationale: A release goal states the change in what a user can do, which is the level at which a quarter of work can be steered and traded off as the quarter gets tight.

options.text: The work breakdown structure
options.rationale: Not used. A breakdown of deliverables describes how the work is divided, not what any of it is for. It answers a planning question, and none of the three above is a planning question.

questions.explanation: Statements of intent operate at different horizons, and reaching for one at the wrong level is a common way for purpose to go missing. Investment justification, dated outcome targets and release-level goals each answer a different question, and none of them is a description of the work itself. When someone cannot say what a piece of work is for, the usual fault is that they have been handed the level below the one they needed.
questions.mindset: Match the statement of intent to the horizon of the decision being taken.

questions.stem: An offshore wind operator runs a turbine-reliability programme with two teams. The data team works in two-week iterations, ships fault-prediction models quickly and accepts a false-alarm rate it intends to tune later. The vessel-scheduling team plans maintenance windows months ahead and treats a false alarm as a wasted sailing costing £14,000. Each team's statement of purpose is coherent on its own. Last week the two made opposite calls on the same alert. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask the data team to hold its releases until the false-alarm rate is low enough for the vessel team to act on every alert it receives.
options.rationale: It resolves the tension by having one team absorb all of it. A model that cannot ship until it is right also loses the operational feedback it needs in order to become right.

options.text: Convene both teams to agree what a false alarm is worth against a missed fault, and state that ratio in the shared purpose.
options.rationale: The teams are not disagreeing about facts but about the relative cost of two errors, which nobody has ranked. Putting the ratio in the shared purpose gives both the same rule for the next alert.

options.text: Give the vessel-scheduling team the final call on any alert, since it is the team that carries the cost of acting.
options.rationale: Handing the decision to whoever feels one cost optimises for avoiding sailings rather than for turbine availability. The team bearing a single kind of loss is the worst placed to weigh it against the other.

options.text: Set a false-alarm threshold from the published industry benchmark and apply it consistently to every alert from now on.
options.rationale: A benchmark imported from other operators encodes their economics, not this one's. It answers the question with a number nobody in the programme has agreed represents their own trade-off.

questions.explanation: Two groups with coherent but separate purposes will make opposite decisions the moment their objectives trade against each other, and the fault lies in neither statement. A shared purpose has to name the exchange rate between the things being traded — what one kind of error is worth against another — because that is precisely what each local statement is silent about. Until the ratio is explicit, every instance of the conflict is settled by whoever happens to be in the room.
questions.mindset: Where two objectives trade against each other, the shared purpose must state the exchange rate.

questions.stem: A water company's mains-renewal programme exists to cut daily leakage from 340 megalitres to 255 megalitres within three years. Eighteen months in, leakage stands at 306 megalitres and the programme has spent 60 per cent of its £48 million budget. The board meets on Thursday. Work out how far through the committed benefit the programme actually is, then say what the two figures together indicate about the account it should be giving.

blanks.label: Total leakage reduction the programme is committed to, in megalitres per day
blanks.rationale: 340 minus 255 is 85 megalitres a day. The commitment is the size of the change, not the level at either end, and every completion figure below is a share of this number.

blanks.label: Reduction achieved so far, in megalitres per day
blanks.rationale: 340 minus 306 is 34 megalitres a day delivered so far. Reading the 306 on its own says nothing, because it has meaning only against the 340 it started from.

blanks.label: Share of the committed reduction delivered, to the nearest whole per cent
blanks.rationale: 34 divided by 85 is 0.40, so 40 per cent of the benefit is delivered against 60 per cent of the budget spent and half the calendar gone.

blanks.label: Is the benefit ahead of, level with, or behind the money spent
blanks.rationale: Forty per cent of the benefit against 60 per cent of the spend puts the benefit behind the money. That comparison is what a board needs, and neither figure alone supports it.

questions.explanation: A purpose expressed as a target only becomes steerable when progress is read as a share of the change committed, rather than as movement away from the starting point. The level alone flatters a programme that began well and stalled; the spend alone says nothing about what was bought. Pairing them is what tells a board whether the work is still on course to deliver what it was funded for, and presenting the pair is the project manager's job rather than the board's.
questions.mindset: Report progress against the size of the change promised, and always beside what it has cost.

questions.stem: A veterinary group's app was built so owners could book appointments without phoning, and the product goal names a reduction in call volume. Six months after launch calls are down only slightly, but 70 per cent of app sessions are owners photographing a wound or a rash and asking whether a visit is needed. Nurses answer these within minutes and like doing it. The product owner proposes rewriting the product goal around triage. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Have the team establish what the triage use is worth to the practices and to owners before the goal is rewritten around it.
options.rationale: Heavy use is evidence of demand, not of value. The goal should move only once somebody can say what the new behaviour delivers, and to whom, in terms the practices themselves recognise.

options.text: Rewrite the product goal around triage now, since the usage data already shows what owners want from the product.
options.rationale: It promotes a usage pattern to a purpose without asking what it is worth. Six months of enthusiastic use can sit quite happily alongside no change in cost, capacity or animal outcomes.

options.text: Hold the existing goal and treat the triage traffic as a distraction from the call-volume outcome the app was funded this year to deliver.
options.rationale: Defending the original goal against evidence turns a plan into a commitment. The usage is telling the team something about the problem, and dismissing it wastes the most direct signal they have.

options.text: Split the product into two goals, one for booking and one for triage, and let the team serve both from one backlog.
options.rationale: Two goals with no priority between them leave every trade-off inside the sprint unresolved. It postpones the decision about what the product is for by writing both answers down.

questions.explanation: Unexpected usage is a finding, not a mandate. Heavy adoption shows that people have a problem; it does not yet say what solving that problem is worth, or to whom, and volume and value come apart routinely. Equally, a goal that no longer matches what people actually do is not protected by having once been approved. Keep the purpose under continuous review and move it on evidence of value rather than evidence of traffic.
questions.mindset: Treat surprising usage as a question about value, not yet as an answer about purpose.

questions.stem: The diagram shows the agreed results chain for a district heating retrofit, running from what the project builds through to what the borough is ultimately pursuing. The project runs for two years and has no control over the borough's wider energy policy. Select the element that the project's objective should be stated and measured against.

graphic.title: Four-stage results chain from deliverable to strategic goal
graphic.caption: Select an element. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between them, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Deliverable — 1,900 flats connected to the heat network
regions.rationale: Completing the connections is the project's output, and it will be complete whether or not a single bill falls. Measuring success here confirms that the work happened, not that it worked.

regions.label: Capability — connected residents able to switch to the network tariff
regions.rationale: A capability is what the output makes possible, and it can sit entirely unused. It is a necessary link in the chain, but a project measured here can succeed while nothing changes for anyone.

regions.label: Outcome — average resident heating bill 18 per cent lower within a year of connection
regions.rationale: This is the first link that states a change in someone's circumstances while still sitting inside the period and the influence of the project. That combination is what an objective has to have.

regions.label: Strategic goal — the borough reaches net zero by 2035
regions.rationale: The strategic goal is what the outcome contributes to, across a portfolio and a horizon the project does not control. Holding the project to it makes success unmeasurable within the project's own life.

questions.explanation: A results chain runs from what a project produces to what its organisation is ultimately pursuing, and the objective belongs at the first link that describes a real change in someone's circumstances while remaining inside the project's horizon and influence. Anchoring it earlier makes delivery the definition of success; anchoring it later makes success something nobody can find true or false until long after the project has closed.
questions.mindset: Anchor the objective at the nearest link that is both a real change and still within reach.

questions.stem: A depot upgrade runs for fourteen months on a working rail maintenance site. The purpose — fewer trains held out of service overnight — is well understood by the day shift, who attend the fortnightly briefing. The night shift of 30 fitters does not: their supervisor relays what he remembers, and last month two crews reworked a bay to a specification the project had abandoned. Night workers are paid from the depot's budget, and the depot manager will not fund attendance at a daytime briefing.

options.text: Ask the depot manager to make the night supervisor a formal member of the project team, with briefing the crews as a duty of the role.
options.rationale: It fixes the relay by promoting the relay. What reaches the crews is still one person's summary at second hand, which is exactly what produced the rework being addressed.

options.text: Record a short briefing each fortnight and require the night shift to watch it together at the start of their shift.
options.rationale: A recording carries the content but not the correction: nobody can ask the question that would have caught the abandoned specification. One-way promotion is where misunderstandings quietly survive.

options.text: Move the briefing to the shift handover where both shifts overlap, and accept the disruption that causes to the day shift's start.
options.rationale: The handover is the one moment both shifts are present and the depot already pays for, so it needs no budget you do not hold. The cost is real and falls on the day shift, which is what makes it a trade you can actually make.

options.text: Escalate to the sponsor to have the night shift's briefing attendance funded from the project budget instead of the depot's.
options.rationale: It buys a solution to a problem a scheduling change would solve, and spends sponsor credibility on a funding argument with a peer. Escalation earns its place when nothing inside your own reach works.

questions.explanation: When part of the workforce cannot reach the forum where purpose is built and corrected, the fix is a change to the forum rather than a better relay or a wider broadcast. Look first for a moment the organisation already pays for — a handover, a shift change, a standing meeting — before asking for money or authority you do not hold. Choosing it means accepting a cost somewhere, and naming who bears that cost is part of making the choice honestly.
questions.mindset: Move the meeting to where the people are before asking anyone to fund moving the people.

questions.stem: Your product team shares an office with eight engineers from the platform supplier, who join your stand-ups and take work from your board. Their own company measures them monthly on tickets closed and pays a bonus on it. They are clearing small tickets quickly and steering around the two pieces of work that would move the product goal, which is cutting the time a stranded driver waits for a recovery vehicle. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Show the supplier's account manager how the ticket measure is steering the engineers away from the outcome their platform was bought for.
options.rationale: The misalignment sits in a measure the supplier owns and nobody inside your project can see. Naming it to the person able to change it turns a behaviour problem into a decision somebody can actually take.

options.text: Ask the engineers to treat their ticket count as secondary to the product goal for as long as they are working on your team.
options.rationale: It asks eight people to choose your goal over their own pay. Even where they agree, the incentive stays in place and the behaviour returns as soon as attention moves elsewhere.

options.text: Agree with the account manager a measure the engineers can be judged on that moves with the driver-wait outcome.
options.rationale: Behaviour follows the measure, so an outcome-linked measure is what makes the supplier's interest and the product's the same thing. It is also the only version of this fix that survives your absence.

options.text: Raise a formal contract issue with procurement about the supplier's internal incentives and how they conflict with the engagement.
options.rationale: A formal issue turns a solvable misalignment into a dispute before anyone has been asked to fix it. It also spends the relationship with a supplier whose engineers you need next week.

options.text: Break the two larger pieces of work into many small tickets so the work fits what the engineers are already measured on.
options.rationale: Reshaping the work to fit a measure you believe is wrong entrenches it. The tickets get closed, the goal is served by accident, and the next substantial piece of work meets the same obstacle.

questions.explanation: People working on a project often answer to a measure set outside it, and when behaviour looks irrational the incentive is usually the explanation. The response is to surface the mismatch to whoever owns that measure and get it changed, rather than asking individuals to act against their own interests or bending the work to fit. Shared purpose across an organisational boundary means both sides can hit their own targets by doing the same thing.
questions.mindset: When behaviour contradicts the goal, look for the measure someone else is being paid against.

questions.stem: A regional manager has become the loudest supporter of your engineer-scheduling project and has told his 200 field engineers that it will end weekend working. Weekend rotas are set by a separate resourcing policy and sit outside your scope; the project reduces travel time, not weekend shifts. His enthusiasm has brought several sceptical depots on board. The first release is eight weeks away and nobody has corrected the claim. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Issue a correction to all 200 field engineers, setting out plainly what the project will change about their working week and what it will not.
options.rationale: Correcting a manager's claim to his own staff over his head costs you the advocate who brought the sceptical depots round. The message can be entirely accurate and still do more damage than the error.

options.text: Say nothing for now, on the basis that the travel-time saving may itself reduce weekend working indirectly once the first release has landed.
options.rationale: It hopes an unfunded side effect will cover a promise nobody made. When the rotas do not change, the disappointment attaches to the project and to him at the same time.

options.text: Add weekend rotas to the project's scope so that the expectation his 200 engineers are now holding can actually be met.
options.rationale: Letting an overstated benefit pull scope inverts the order: what the project is for stops driving what it does. It also commits the project to a policy area it does not own.

options.text: Speak to the regional manager, show him what the project does and does not change, and agree how he puts it right with his depots.
options.rationale: He made the claim and holds the standing with those engineers, so he is the one who can withdraw it without losing them. Doing it together keeps the correction accurate and keeps the advocate.

questions.explanation: A supporter who overstates the benefit is a larger risk than a sceptic, because the disappointment arrives later and attaches to the project. The correction belongs with the person who made the claim: they own the relationship it was made inside, and a public correction issued around them repairs the facts while costing you the advocacy. Promoting a purpose includes policing its edges, because what the work will not do is part of what it is.
questions.mindset: Correct an overstatement through the person who made it, not around them.

questions.stem: A ferry operator's service-improvement programme exists so that islanders can rely on reaching the mainland for hospital appointments. Its headline measure is the share of sailings departing within ten minutes of schedule, now up from 71 to 88 per cent. Crews are achieving it partly by closing the vehicle deck early, and complaints from passengers left standing on the quay have tripled since spring. The crews are doing exactly what they were asked to do.

options.text: Instruct crews to hold departure for any passenger present on the quay, whatever that does to the punctuality figure.
options.rationale: It asks crews to fail a measure they are judged against on the project manager's say-so. The instruction is also unenforceable the moment nobody senior is watching the ramp.

options.text: Investigate the complaints to establish how many of the passengers left behind had arrived before the advertised closing time.
options.rationale: It treats a known cause as though it still needed proving. The crews' behaviour is not in doubt, and the investigation spends weeks confirming what the measure already explains.

options.text: Add a passengers-carried measure of equal standing to punctuality and report the two together as the programme's headline.
options.rationale: Any single measure of a service will be optimised at the expense of what it omits. Pairing it with the thing being sacrificed keeps the behaviour honest without asking anyone to ignore their target.

options.text: Replace the punctuality measure with an islander satisfaction survey that captures the experience the programme exists to improve.
options.rationale: A survey describes the outcome but arrives months after the sailing and cannot steer a decision taken at the ramp. Trading a gameable measure for an unactionable one loses the grip the programme has gained.

questions.explanation: Any measure standing in for a purpose will be optimised, including in the ways it fails to capture; this is a property of measurement rather than a failure of the people being measured. The remedy is a balancing measure at the same standing as the first, so the sacrifice shows up in the same report as the gain. Removing the measure, or exhorting people past it, leaves the incentive intact and the purpose no better served.
questions.mindset: Assume any proxy for the purpose will be optimised, and pair it with what it would otherwise cost.

questions.stem: Each sentence below describes a moment three months into a community radio platform rebuild, at which the team's grip on what the product is for has started to slip. Complete each one with the response that fits the situation. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Three weeks of stand-ups have run entirely on ticket status and nobody has mentioned the product goal in any of them. The project manager should
The product goal has been met three weeks before the release it was written for, and the backlog still holds the items planned for those weeks. The project manager should

options.text: open the stand-up with the measure the goal moves, and ask what the day's work does to it
options.rationale: A goal that is never referenced stops informing decisions within weeks, whatever people can still recall of it. Putting the measure at the top of a meeting that already happens is the cheapest way to keep it in use.

options.text: ask the product owner to set the next goal now, rather than working through the remaining planned items
options.rationale: Those items were planned to serve a goal that is already achieved, so their justification has gone with it. A goal met early is an opportunity to re-aim, not a licence to finish the list.

options.text: run a retrospective into why the estimates were wrong
options.rationale: Not used. Neither situation is about estimation: one is a goal falling out of daily use, and the other is what to do with time freed by reaching it sooner than planned.

questions.explanation: A purpose decays through disuse rather than disagreement, so the routine meetings are where it is either kept live or quietly lost. And work planned in service of a goal loses its justification when the goal is reached, which makes an early finish a moment to ask what the next thing worth doing is. In both cases the corrective is to put the goal back into the decision rather than to carry on executing the plan around it.
questions.mindset: Plans serve goals, so when the goal changes state the plan stops being self-justifying.

questions.stem: A brewery is replacing its bottling line. The objective is usable output of 24,000 bottles an hour, and the line must be commissioned before the Christmas run begins on 3 November. For two months every design question has been settled by asking what protects 3 November, and the team has accepted three compromises that each shave throughput. Nobody has proposed moving the date. The next such decision, on the labelling head, is on Friday.

options.text: State the throughput objective as the decision rule, and require any compromise that reduces it to be raised as a change with its cost.
options.rationale: Setting how technical decisions are taken sits inside the project manager's remit and needs nobody's permission. It makes each trade visible at the moment it is made rather than in the commissioning report.

options.text: Take the three accepted compromises to the sponsor with a recommendation that the commissioning date should be moved back.
options.rationale: It offers the sponsor one answer to a question about trade-offs, and the date may well be the constraint that genuinely cannot move. The problem is how decisions are being taken, which a later date does not fix.

options.text: Model the combined throughput effect of the three compromises before changing anything about the way these decisions are taken.
options.rationale: The modelling is worth doing, but Friday's decision arrives first and the pattern repeats while the analysis runs. Understanding the damage is not the same as stopping it.

options.text: Add the throughput objective to the design review checklist so that it is weighed alongside the 3 November date at each of the remaining gates.
options.rationale: A checklist entry puts the objective in the room without saying what happens when it loses. A hard constraint beats a soft objective every time unless the order between them is stated explicitly.

questions.explanation: A hard constraint will quietly become the objective unless somebody states the relationship between them, because a date is unambiguous and a benefit is not. The project manager does not need permission to set how decisions are taken: naming the objective as the decision rule, and making any erosion of it a visible change rather than a design detail, restores the order without reopening the constraint. A deadline is a boundary the purpose is pursued within.
questions.mindset: A deadline is a boundary on the objective, and left unstated it will replace it.

questions.stem: A charity's team is rebuilding, in fortnightly releases, the platform matching supermarket surplus to food banks. The purpose is agreed: less edible food wasted, more of it reaching households inside its shelf life. Match each audience to the version of that purpose that gives them something to act on. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Warehouse volunteers deciding which pallets to sort first on a Tuesday morning.
The funder's trustees deciding whether to release the second year of the grant.
A supermarket partner's regional manager deciding whether to extend the scheme to 40 more stores.

options.text: Sort by remaining shelf life, because a pallet that misses its window feeds nobody
options.rationale: A volunteer needs the purpose as a rule that settles the next hour's work. Shelf life is the part of the purpose their particular choice actually moves.

options.text: Tonnes redistributed inside shelf life per pound of grant, against the year-one baseline
options.rationale: Trustees are deciding whether the money bought the outcome, so the purpose has to arrive as outcome per unit of the funding they are being asked to commit again.

options.text: Disposal cost avoided per store, and the collection slot each store would need to give up
options.rationale: A regional manager is deciding whether to commit staff and space, so the purpose has to appear in the terms their own operation is judged on, without its substance changing.

options.text: A case study of one family helped by the scheme last winter
options.rationale: Not used. A single story moves feeling but decides nothing. None of these three audiences is choosing whether to care; each of them is choosing what to do next.

questions.explanation: One purpose has to reach audiences taking entirely different decisions, and it reaches them by being expressed in the units of the decision in front of them — while its substance stays identical between versions. If two audiences would act incompatibly on their own version, the purpose has been altered rather than translated. The test of a good translation is that everyone, acting on the version they were given, pulls the same way.
questions.mindset: Express the purpose in the units of the decision the listener is about to take.

questions.stem: You run an eleven-month programme building an in-house scheduling system for a chain of 40 dental practices, justified by saving £1.2 million a year in missed appointments. Four months in, with £400,000 spent, a supplier launches a product that independent trials suggest would deliver most of that saving for £90,000 a year. Your sponsor commissioned the in-house build personally and the team is performing well. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Continue the build and run a supplier evaluation in parallel, so that the comparison costs the programme no schedule.
options.rationale: Parallel running sounds prudent but it spends the build's money while the question stays open, and a team that suspects it may be cancelled does not perform as it did. It defers the decision at full price.

options.text: Complete the current stage to a working increment, then compare the two options using real evidence from your own product.
options.rationale: Better evidence is worth something, but four more months of spend to sharpen a comparison already decisive on price is an expensive way to be certain. A stage boundary is a schedule artefact, not an information threshold.

options.text: Raise the supplier's product as a risk to the business case and put it to the next programme board on the standing agenda.
options.rationale: Routing it as a risk understates it: this is a challenge to whether the programme should exist at all, and a standing agenda gives it the ten minutes a risk gets. The form of an escalation sets the seriousness of its hearing.

options.text: Put the business case back to the sponsor now, with the £400,000 treated as spent either way, and ask for a continue-or-stop decision.
options.rationale: The justification for the programme is the saving, and something else may now deliver it, which puts the case rather than the plan in question. Setting the £400,000 aside lets the sponsor decide on the next pound rather than defend the last one.

questions.explanation: A purpose is a claim that this work is the best available way to obtain a particular benefit, and events during delivery can falsify that claim. When they do, the item under review is the business case rather than the schedule or the risk register, and it belongs to whoever approved it, framed as continue or stop. Money already spent is not a reason to continue, and a sponsor's personal investment is a reason to be careful how the question is put, not whether to put it.
questions.mindset: The business case is a live claim, and information that breaks it is a reason to reopen it rather than to log it.

questions.stem: A cycle-hire app team holds a product goal of letting a rider find and unlock a bike in under sixty seconds. At Thursday's stand-up a developer mentions that the identity check he has been asked to add to the unlock flow takes most riders around ninety seconds on a first hire, and that he is a day from finishing it. Nobody in the room had connected the two before he said it. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Let him finish the identity check as specified, and put the conflict on the agenda for the sprint retrospective.
options.rationale: It spends a day building something already known to work against the goal, and sends the question to a forum held after the decision mattered. Retrospectives improve the next sprint, not this one.

options.text: Get the developer and the product owner together today to settle whether the check can meet the goal or the goal must move.
options.rationale: A clash between a requirement and the goal is a decision, and the product owner owns it. Both people are available today, so there is no reason for the question to wait a single sprint.

options.text: Record it as a defect against the unlock flow so that it is prioritised through the team's normal backlog route.
options.rationale: Calling it a defect files a question about intent as a fault in the build. It will then be triaged on severity rather than answered on whether the product still does what it promises.

options.text: Ask the developer to get the identity check under sixty seconds before he finishes and submits the story.
options.rationale: It assumes the goal wins without anyone asking why the check was required. An unlock flow that misses a compliance need is not a faster product, it is an unusable one.

questions.explanation: When a requirement and the goal are found to contradict each other, the contradiction is a decision and it belongs to whoever owns the goal. Deferring it to a scheduled forum, reclassifying it as a fault, or resolving it yourself in favour of either side all bypass the person who can weigh the two. The moment to raise it is the moment it is noticed, because that is while both options are still cheap.
questions.mindset: A clash between the work and the goal is news, and news travels the same day.

questions.stem: The signed charter for a regional airport's security-lane refurbishment states the objective as improving the passenger experience. Planning starts in two weeks. The sponsor is available, the operations team holds queue-time data by half-hour, and the airport publishes a service standard committing to 95 per cent of passengers cleared within ten minutes. Which two actions should the project manager take before planning begins?

options.text: Plan against the charter as written, and let a working definition of a good passenger experience emerge as the design develops.
options.rationale: It begins planning with no way to tell whether one design option is better than another. Definitions that emerge during design tend to be the ones that justify the design already preferred.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to reissue the charter with a fuller description of the passenger experience the airport is aiming at.
options.rationale: Sending the problem back unworked asks the sponsor to do the drafting. A vague objective usually stays vague when the person who wrote it is asked to try again without help.

options.text: Draft a measurable objective from the queue-time data and the published service standard, and put it to the sponsor to confirm.
options.rationale: Turning a stated intention into something measurable is the project manager's work, and the raw material already exists. Taking it back for confirmation keeps the objective the sponsor's while making it usable.

options.text: Commission passenger research to establish which aspects of the experience matter most before any objective is agreed.
options.rationale: Research would be justified if nothing were known, but a published standard and half-hourly queue data already state what the airport counts. It buys weeks to rediscover what is on file.

options.text: Agree with the sponsor which aspects of the passenger experience the refurbishment will not touch, and record them.
options.rationale: An objective is defined as much by its edges as its content. Naming what the work will not cover stops an unbounded phrase being quoted back later as a promise about all of it.

questions.explanation: An objective that cannot be found true or false is not yet an objective, and converting one into measurable terms is the project manager's job rather than grounds for sending the charter back. The raw material is usually already in the organisation, in the standards it publishes and the data it keeps. Fixing the boundary matters as much as fixing the measure, because a broad phrase left unbounded will be read later as a commitment to everything inside it.
questions.mindset: Make a vague objective measurable yourself, then have its owner confirm it.

questions.stem: A council is replacing 18,000 street-light columns over four years. The objective in the approved plan reads: reduce complaints about dark streets. At the first design workshop an engineer asks what a good result actually looks like, and nobody can answer beyond fewer complaints. Complaints are logged by ward rather than by column, and the council publishes no lighting standard. The design options differ mainly in how evenly they light a street. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Set a target reduction in complaints — half the current volume by year two — so that the objective at least has a number attached to it.
options.rationale: Putting a number on the wrong quantity makes it harder to challenge rather than easier. Complaints count how many people bothered to report something, which moves with weather, publicity and trust in the council.

options.text: Work up a positive statement of the lighting result the council wants, and take it to the sponsor to approve as the objective.
options.rationale: A project needs a description of the condition it is creating before it can compare design options at all. Drafting it and having the sponsor approve it turns an absence of direction into a decision.

options.text: Proceed with the design options and let the complaint data from the first ward's installation show which of the approaches performs best in practice.
options.rationale: It defers the definition of success until 4,500 columns are already in the ground. The first ward is a commitment rather than an experiment, and its complaint data arrives far too late to steer the rest.

options.text: Ask the complaints team to start recording which column each complaint relates to, so that the objective can be measured accurately.
options.rationale: Better data about complaints refines a proxy instead of replacing it. The project would end up measuring precisely something that is not what the council is trying to achieve.

questions.explanation: An objective framed as the removal of a symptom cannot steer a design, because it says nothing about the condition being created and every option removes some of the symptom. What is needed is a description of the intended end state, drafted by the project manager and signed off by whoever owns the work. Measuring a proxy more precisely makes it more accurate without making it any more relevant.
questions.mindset: State what the project is creating, not only what it is meant to make go away.

questions.stem: Your team is six weeks into building a self-service energy-account tool, with a product goal of cutting billing calls by a third. Two developers have told you separately that they think customers ring because the bills themselves are confusing, and that the tool will not touch that. Neither has said so in any team forum, and their work has slowed noticeably. The product owner has heard none of this. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask the two developers to put their argument to the product owner directly, and help them assemble the call patterns they have observed.
options.rationale: A doubt that only circulates privately cannot be tested or answered, and it is already showing in the work. Getting it in front of the person who owns the goal makes it either a correction or a settled question.

options.text: Explain to the developers that the goal was agreed with the sponsor, and ask them to commit to it for the current release.
options.rationale: Asking for commitment before the objection has been heard buys compliance and leaves the belief intact. The slowing work is a symptom of that belief, and restating the hierarchy will not speed it up.

options.text: Take the concern to the product owner yourself, so that the two developers are not exposed if their argument turns out to be unpopular.
options.rationale: Relaying it second hand strips the observation of the detail that makes it persuasive, and teaches the team that dissent travels through you. It also leaves the developers unable to answer the obvious follow-up questions.

options.text: Add a billing-clarity item to the backlog so that the concern is visibly acted on while the product goal itself stays exactly as it is.
options.rationale: It answers a challenge about whether the goal is right by adding scope. The team gets a gesture, the goal keeps an assumption nobody has examined, and the backlog gains an item with no owner.

questions.explanation: Disagreement about what a project is for does not disappear when it goes unspoken; it turns into slow work and quiet hedging. The response is to route the objection to whoever owns the goal, in the words of the people who hold it, because they are the only ones who can answer the questions that follow. A purpose never tested against its strongest internal critic is being taken on trust.
questions.mindset: Unspoken disagreement about the goal is still disagreement, and it shows in the work before it shows in a meeting.

questions.stem: A fire and rescue service is deploying mobile data terminals in 40 appliances. The business case claims 90 seconds off average mobilisation, but two-thirds of that saving depends on the control room changing how it despatches — a change your project has no mandate to make and which nobody in control has agreed to own. Go-live is in five months. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Ask the sponsor to name an owner in control-room operations who is accountable for the despatch change and the saving it carries.
options.rationale: Two-thirds of the benefit sits outside the project's mandate, so somebody with authority in that function has to own it. Naming them is a decision only the sponsor can take, and it is what makes the benefit real.

options.text: Reduce the claimed benefit in the business case to the 30 seconds that the terminals deliver on their own.
options.rationale: It protects the project's reporting by quietly shrinking what the organisation was promised. The saving is still available, and writing it out of the case abandons it rather than pursuing it.

options.text: Deliver the terminals as planned and raise the despatch dependency as a finding at the post-implementation review.
options.rationale: The review happens after the money is spent and the opportunity has passed. A dependency known five months ahead and raised afterwards was a decision not to manage it.

options.text: Add the despatch change to the plan as a dependency with its own date, so that it is visible beside the technical delivery.
options.rationale: A dependency that is not on the plan is invisible on every status report until it fails. Giving it a date and a place alongside the build is what lets anyone see it slipping in time to act.

options.text: Have your team design the new despatch process and present it to the control-room managers as a finished part of the deployment package.
options.rationale: Designing another function's process produces something nobody in control has agreed to and cannot be made to adopt. Ownership is not transferred by handing over a finished answer.

questions.explanation: A benefit that depends on somebody else changing how they work is not delivered by the project that builds the tool, and the space between output and outcome is where most business cases quietly fail. The work is to have an owner named inside that function and to put their change on the plan with a date, so the dependency stays visible while there is time. Shrinking the claim settles the question by giving the benefit up.
questions.mindset: If the benefit needs someone else to change, the project is not finished when the thing is built.

questions.stem: A foundry must fit emissions abatement to meet a permit condition by 31 March or stop casting. The approved case also claims a 12 per cent energy saving that only the larger heat-recovery option delivers, and that option now looks likely to miss March by about three weeks. The smaller option meets the permit comfortably and returns roughly a fifth of the energy saving. Your engineering lead wants to press on with the larger one.

options.text: Press on with the larger option and open a three-week permit extension request with the regulator in parallel, so both objectives stay in play.
options.rationale: It puts a licence to operate in the hands of a regulator with no obligation to agree. Treating a hard constraint as negotiable because the benefit is attractive is how a project loses both of them.

options.text: Switch to the smaller option now and write the energy saving out of the business case, since the permit is what the business cannot survive missing.
options.rationale: The first half is right and the second gives away a benefit that remains achievable later. Abandoning an objective because it cannot be reached by one date confuses the deadline with the goal.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to choose between the permit date and the energy saving, setting out the consequences of each for the foundry.
options.rationale: It presents a genuine constraint as though it were an option on a menu. A permit condition is not a preference the sponsor can trade, and offering it as one wastes the escalation.

options.text: Fit the smaller abatement to secure the permit by March, and take heat recovery forward as a second phase with its own case.
options.rationale: The permit is a constraint and the saving is an objective, so the constraint sets the boundary and the objective is pursued as far as that boundary allows. Phasing keeps the benefit alive instead of trading it away.

questions.explanation: Constraints and objectives are different kinds of thing, and the recurring failure is weighing one against the other. A constraint bounds the solution space; an objective is what you maximise inside it. Where a benefit cannot be had within the boundary by the date, the question is whether it can be had later — not whether the boundary might move, and not whether the benefit should be written off.
questions.mindset: Satisfy the constraint, then pursue the objective as far as the constraint allows.

questions.stem: A cinema chain's team has had four product goals in four sprints: faster seat selection, then loyalty sign-ups, then fewer refund requests, then screen-time accuracy. Each was a reasonable response to something a director said that fortnight. The team has shipped small pieces of all four and finished none of them. At today's sprint planning the product owner introduces a fifth. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask the product owner to rank the five goals, so that the team knows which takes precedence whenever any two of them conflict.
options.rationale: Ranking five goals still leaves five goals. The team would go on spreading a fortnight across all of them, now with a stated order to feel guilty about rather than one thing to finish.

options.text: Raise it at the retrospective, where the team can describe for themselves the effect the constant changes are having on their ability to finish anything.
options.rationale: The pattern is already visible and the fifth goal is being set in this meeting. Waiting for the retrospective spends another fortnight before the conversation happens at all.

options.text: Ask the product owner what the product itself should achieve over the coming quarter, and hold each of the sprint goals beneath it.
options.rationale: A product goal has a horizon longer than a sprint, which is what allows sprint goals to add up to something. Establishing the longer aim gives each fortnightly request somewhere to be judged.

options.text: Ask the directors to route their requests through the product owner rather than raising them with the team during the sprint.
options.rationale: Channelling the requests tidies the route without changing the behaviour at the end of it. The product owner is already the person converting each request into a new goal.

questions.explanation: Levels of intent have different lifespans: a product goal spans many sprints and a sprint goal spans one, and that gap is what lets short cycles accumulate into something. When the longer statement is rewritten at the cadence of the shorter one, a team is left with a run of unfinished starts and no basis on which to judge the next request. Responsiveness is a property of what gets built, not of what the work is for.
questions.mindset: Each level of intent has a lifespan, and a goal rewritten every sprint is not a goal.

questions.stem: A bus operator's statement of purpose for its ticketing replacement makes three claims about what the new system will achieve, and the board has asked how each of them will be shown to be true. Match each claim to the evidence that would demonstrate it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Passengers will spend less time boarding.
Drivers will spend less of the working day handling cash.
The operator will be able to tell within a week which routes are losing money.

options.text: Mean dwell time per stop, sampled on the same routes before and after
options.rationale: Boarding time is a duration, so the evidence has to be a duration measured the same way on both sides of the change. Using the same routes controls for the obvious alternative explanations.

options.text: Share of journeys paid in cash, with the time booked to cash reconciliation per shift
options.rationale: The claim is about how drivers spend their day, so it needs the volume of cash journeys and the effort booked against handling them. Either figure can move on its own without the claim being true.

options.text: The date the first weekly route-margin report is produced from live data
options.rationale: A claim about a capability is demonstrated by the capability existing and being used, which is a date rather than a trend. Whether the report is any good is a separate question from whether it exists.

options.text: The number of passengers who have registered a smartcard account
options.rationale: Not used. Registrations count how many people signed up, which is activity on the way to a result rather than a result. The figure would rise even if boarding, cash handling and reporting were all unchanged.

questions.explanation: Each claim in a statement of purpose implies a particular kind of evidence, and the common error is accepting a measure of activity in place of a measure of the claim. A claim about duration needs a duration; a claim about how time is spent needs both volume and effort; a claim about a capability is answered by whether it exists and is used. Asking what would show a claim false is usually quicker than asking what would show it true.
questions.mindset: For every claim in the purpose, name the evidence that would settle it either way.

questions.stem: A zoo is introducing automated feed preparation across eight keeper teams. The case rests on consistency of diets and two hours a day returned to animal observation. Keepers prepare feeds by hand today, and several have said in workshops that the preparation hour is precisely when they notice an animal is off colour. The head keeper supports the project. You are drafting the statement of purpose every team will be briefed on.

options.text: State the purpose as more time with the animals, and let the observation benefit answer the keepers' concern about preparation on its own.
options.rationale: It offers the benefit and passes over the loss, which the keepers have already named out loud. A purpose that ignores a cost its audience can see is heard as a sales pitch and discounted accordingly.

options.text: State the purpose as better observation, name what the preparation hour contributes to it, and say how that will be replaced.
options.rationale: The concern is not an obstacle to the purpose; it is information about how observation currently happens. Naming it and saying what carries it afterwards is what makes the statement survive contact with the people doing the work.

options.text: Leave the preparation hour out of the statement and handle the concern through the head keeper in team conversations instead.
options.rationale: Routing an unresolved point through one supporter keeps it out of the written purpose and out of the record. The keepers then hear two accounts, and the quieter one is the honest one.

options.text: Delay the statement until a trial in one keeper team shows whether observation quality actually holds up without the preparation hour.
options.rationale: A trial would produce useful evidence, but the teams are being briefed now and the statement is what they will judge the project by. Silence while the trial runs is itself a message about their point.

questions.explanation: A statement of purpose is read by the people whose work it changes, and they know what the change costs before it is written down. Naming what is being given up, and saying what will carry that function afterwards, separates a purpose people can argue with from one they simply discount. The content of an objection is usually a description of how the current system really works, which the case for change tends not to capture.
questions.mindset: Write the purpose so that the people who lose something can still recognise it as true.

questions.stem: A clothing retailer's returns programme exists to cut the time between a parcel arriving and the item becoming resellable from 9 days to 3. Two of its four workstreams are complete and together took the figure to 6 days. Funding has now been cut and only one of the two remaining workstreams can proceed: automated grading would take a further 2 days off, re-siting the photo studio a further 1 day. Work the figures through.

blanks.label: Total reduction the programme is committed to, in days
blanks.rationale: Nine days down to three is a commitment to remove six days. Progress has to be read against that figure rather than against the nine days it started from.

blanks.label: Reduction delivered by the first two workstreams, in days
blanks.rationale: Nine days to six is three days removed, which is half of the committed reduction from half of the workstreams.

blanks.label: Share of the committed reduction met if automated grading proceeds, to the nearest whole per cent
blanks.rationale: Three days already removed plus a further two is five of the six committed, which is 83 per cent. The programme would finish at 4 days against a target of 3.

blanks.label: Which workstream leaves more of the objective unmet if it is the one dropped
blanks.rationale: Dropping grading leaves the programme two days short of the target, against one day short if the studio move is dropped instead. Grading is therefore the workstream whose loss costs the objective most.

questions.explanation: When funding forces a choice between remaining pieces of work, the comparison that matters is how much of the committed change each one preserves — not what each costs, and not how far the work has already come. Expressing every option as a share of the original commitment keeps the objective rather than the budget as the thing being decided about, and it makes plain that finishing at 83 per cent is a shortfall somebody still has to accept.
questions.mindset: Score every descoping option by how much of the promised change it leaves standing.

questions.stem: A seed-testing laboratory's team has spent three of its first four weeks refining a vision statement. The sixth version is on the wall and the team is now arguing about whether the word rapid should be accurate. Two customer laboratories are waiting to try the sample-tracking prototype and have been waiting a fortnight. The product owner thinks one more session will settle it. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask the sponsor to choose between the two remaining wordings, so that the argument has an authoritative end and the team can move on.
options.rationale: It settles a word by escalation without settling anything the word is about. The team gets a ruling and still holds no evidence about which of the two customers actually value.

options.text: Accept the current version as final and move the team on to the prototype, on the basis that six versions is already more than enough.
options.rationale: Closing the argument by decree gets the work moving and leaves the disagreement intact underneath it. The wording matters here because rapid and accurate imply materially different products.

options.text: Facilitate one more session using a structured technique, so that the team reaches an actual decision rather than producing a seventh draft.
options.rationale: Better facilitation of the same conversation produces a better-run version of it. The question is not being answered in the room because the information needed to answer it is not in the room.

options.text: Put the prototype in front of the two waiting laboratories, and let what they turn out to value settle the wording.
options.rationale: The disagreement is about what customers want, which is a question with an external answer. Getting that evidence costs less than another session and resolves the point rather than merely closing it.

questions.explanation: A statement of purpose is a hypothesis about what matters to somebody outside the room, so arguments about its wording are usually arguments about that hypothesis. By the sixth version, more discussion is not converging on anything, because nobody present holds the information required. The quickest route to a shared purpose is often the cheapest piece of contact with the people it is supposed to be about.
questions.mindset: When a team cannot agree on what matters, ask the people it is meant to matter to.

questions.stem: A driving-test agency's booking replacement states its objective as a fall in the share of candidates waiting more than six weeks for a test. Waiting times move sharply with seasonal demand, and a full booking cycle takes six months. The timeline shows four points after delivery. Select the earliest point at which the objective can honestly be judged.

graphic.title: Post-delivery timeline with four candidate measurement points
graphic.caption: Select a point on the timeline. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between them, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Final release deployed — month 14
regions.rationale: Deployment is the point at which the output exists. No candidate has yet booked a test under the new system, so nothing about waiting times can be read from this date.

regions.label: Handover to operations complete — month 15
regions.rationale: Handover marks the end of the project's responsibility rather than the arrival of the outcome. Treating it as the measurement point is how projects come to close before anyone knows whether they worked.

regions.label: First full booking cycle completed — month 21
regions.rationale: A full cycle is the first point at which the measure spans the seasonal variation that drives it. Any figure taken before then compares two different parts of the year.

regions.label: Annual service report published — month 27
regions.rationale: The annual report is a convenient moment rather than a necessary one. Waiting for it adds six months during which a correctable shortfall goes unnoticed by anybody.

questions.explanation: The earliest honest measurement point is set by the natural cycle of whatever is being measured, not by the project's own milestones or the organisation's reporting calendar. Measuring before a full cycle compares unlike periods; waiting for the next convenient report delays the moment anything can be done about a shortfall. Knowing that date at the outset also tells you who needs to still be watching when it arrives.
questions.mindset: An outcome can first be judged after one full cycle of whatever drives it, not when the project finishes.

questions.stem: A national park authority is building 300 parking spaces and a shuttle hub, justified by an objective of reducing verge parking on six lanes. The case rests on a 2019 survey showing that most visitors arrive by car from within 40 miles. Since the new rail halt opened, the ranger team reports that a growing share now arrive on foot from the station and walk those same lanes. Detailed design starts in a month.

options.text: Commission a short count of how visitors actually arrive now, and test the objective against it before the design is fixed.
options.rationale: The case rests on a fact about arrivals that may have changed, and a month is enough to establish it. Checking the assumption is far cheaper before the design commits than after the tarmac is laid.

options.text: Proceed with the design and add the pedestrian question to the risk register for review at the next stage gate, alongside the design itself.
options.rationale: It logs a challenge to the objective as a risk to the plan. By the next gate the design is the thing under discussion, and the objective has quietly stopped being examined at all.

options.text: Ask the ranger team to record verge-parking incidents, so that the objective's own baseline is properly evidenced before design begins.
options.rationale: It measures the symptom the objective names without testing the explanation underneath it. A better baseline for verge parking says nothing about whether parking spaces are what reduces it.

options.text: Raise the rail halt with the sponsor as a change in circumstances, and ask whether the objective ought to be revisited before design.
options.rationale: Taking a question to the sponsor before you have the answer puts them in the position of guessing. The count is a month's work and would turn the question into a decision they can actually take.

questions.explanation: Every objective rests on an assumption about why the problem exists, and those assumptions age. When something in the environment changes that could break one, the cheap move is to test the assumption directly — rather than logging it, measuring the symptom more precisely, or escalating a doubt with no evidence attached. The test of whether an assumption is worth checking is what being wrong about it would cost once the design is fixed.
questions.mindset: An objective is only as current as the assumption under it, so check the assumption when the world moves.

questions.stem: A charity's digital team is six sprints into a platform meant to get more teenage girls into weekly sport. The product goal, the personas and the backlog were all written by charity staff and the funder. No teenage girl has been in any session. Sign-ups are running at a third of forecast. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Commission a survey of teenage girls in the three pilot boroughs, to test the assumptions built into the personas the team works from.
options.rationale: A survey answers the questions the team already thought to ask, which are the questions that produced the personas. It confirms the existing frame rather than exposing what is missing from it.

options.text: Get a small group of teenage girls into the next two sprint reviews, with the goal itself open to their comment.
options.rationale: The gap is that the people the goal is about have never tested it. Putting them where decisions are actually made, rather than in a consultation running alongside, is what lets the goal change.

options.text: Ask the funder to relax the sign-up forecast until the team has had more time to learn what works with this group.
options.rationale: It treats a signal that the goal may be wrong as a reporting problem. Relieving the pressure removes the prompt to investigate and leaves the underlying assumption untouched.

options.text: Run a retrospective on why the personas were written without input from the group they describe, so the team can improve its practice.
options.rationale: Examining how the team arrived here is worth doing later and does nothing about six sprints built on untested personas. The sign-up shortfall is happening now.

options.text: Treat the sign-up shortfall as evidence about the goal itself rather than about the marketing, and say so plainly to the sponsor.
options.rationale: A third of forecast is the clearest information the project has about whether its premise holds. Naming it as a question about the goal, before anyone is asked to promote harder, keeps the real issue in view.

questions.explanation: A purpose written entirely by the people funding and delivering it is a hypothesis about a group who have never seen it. The correction is contact at the point where decisions are taken, not consultation arranged beside them, and it means reading a shortfall as evidence about the premise rather than as a failure of execution. Personas describing people nobody has met are a record of the team's own assumptions.
questions.mindset: If the people the purpose is about have never seen it, it is a guess with a document around it.

questions.stem: A payroll bureau is consolidating four processing platforms into one. The objective — cutting cost per payslip by 22 per cent — cannot be observed until the last client migrates in two years. The programme is nine months in, the board's monthly report shows only milestones and spend, and two sponsors have started asking whether the saving is real. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Explain to the board that the saving is structural and cannot honestly be shown until the final client migration completes in two years.
options.rationale: It is accurate, and it leaves the board with nothing to judge for two years. Confidence with no evidence to renew it decays, and the question will come back louder each quarter.

options.text: Ask the sponsors what evidence would reassure them, and build the next board report around whatever they say would convince them.
options.rationale: It shapes reporting to reassure rather than to inform, and the measures would change with the audience. It also hands the design of the evidence to the people it is meant to persuade.

options.text: Report cost per payslip for the clients already migrated each month, alongside the count of clients still to be moved.
options.rationale: The saving is observable now on the part of the estate that has moved, and the remaining count states how much is still to come. Together they turn a two-year promise into something checkable monthly.

options.text: Bring forward the migration of the two largest clients, so that a meaningful part of the saving becomes visible to the board sooner.
options.rationale: Resequencing a migration to improve reporting lets the report drive the plan. The largest clients are usually sequenced late for reasons that have not gone away.

questions.explanation: A benefit that only appears at the end of a programme still has to be visible during it, or support erodes well before the evidence arrives. The usual source is the subset of work where the outcome can already be observed, reported beside the amount outstanding. Choosing and publishing that measure sits within the project manager's own gift, and it beats both explaining the wait and reshaping the plan around the reporting.
