questions.mindset: Find the part of the benefit that is already observable, and report it beside what is still to come.

questions.stem: A hotel group is rolling out housekeeping scheduling across 30 properties, with the purpose stated as giving housekeepers a predictable finish time. Each general manager briefs it locally. At the Manchester property the manager has told her team it is about getting rooms ready before the 3 p.m. check-in, and her staff are being assigned overlapping rooms as a result. Occupancy there is the highest in the group.

options.text: Reissue the group purpose statement to all 30 general managers, making the predictable finish time unambiguous and asking each to rebrief.
options.rationale: A rebrief to thirty managers treats one local divergence as a general communication failure. It corrects nothing at the property that has actually drifted and tells the other twenty-nine they got it wrong.

options.text: Ask the group's operations director to instruct the Manchester manager to brief the purpose exactly as it is written for everyone else.
options.rationale: Enforcing the wording through the hierarchy produces compliance in the briefing and leaves the scheduling behaviour unexplained. She had a reason, and nobody has yet asked what it was.

options.text: Adopt the Manchester framing across the group, since check-in readiness is plainly what the highest-occupancy property needs.
options.rationale: It promotes one site's adaptation to group purpose on the strength of that site's circumstances. Twenty-nine properties would inherit a goal shaped by a constraint they do not share.

options.text: Go to Manchester and find out what is actually driving her framing before deciding whether this is drift or a real local constraint.
options.rationale: The same divergence can be a misunderstanding or a signal that the group purpose does not fit a real condition. Which it is decides whether you correct the site or revisit the statement.

questions.explanation: A purpose briefed locally will be adapted locally, and adaptation is not automatically drift. Some local versions are misunderstandings and some are evidence that the group statement never accounted for a real condition, and from head office the two look identical. Going to look before choosing between correction and revision is what stops you enforcing a statement that does not work, or generalising a local fix that does not travel.
questions.mindset: A local version of the purpose is evidence before it is an error.

questions.stem: Each sentence describes a moment during a boat builder's move to digital build tracking, at which what the work is for has become unclear to somebody who matters. Complete each one with the response that fits the situation. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A newly appointed operations director asks for a one-line statement of what the programme is for, and there are three approved objectives of roughly equal weight. The project manager should
A second programme starts in the same workshop in the same month with its own purpose, and the fitters cannot tell which initiative a given change belongs to. The project manager should

options.text: give the single objective that the other two serve, and offer the full three immediately afterwards
options.rationale: A one-line answer listing three things is not a one-line answer, and declining to give one reads as evasion. Naming the objective the others support is honest compression, and the rest follows straight away.

options.text: agree a joint account of both programmes with the other project manager and brief the workshop once
options.rationale: The confusion is produced by two initiatives arriving separately, so neither can fix it alone. A single briefing covering both is what lets a fitter place any change they are asked to make.

options.text: ask the fitters to check the programme name on each change request before acting on it
options.rationale: Not used. Labelling moves the work of telling two purposes apart onto the people who were never told how they differ, and it answers neither of the situations above.

questions.explanation: Purpose has to be usable by whoever is asking, which means surviving compression for an executive and collision with whatever else lands on the same people. Three objectives of equal weight usually still have one that the others serve, and where two initiatives share an audience the account they receive should be shared too. Confusion at the receiving end is a fault in how purpose was sent, not in who received it.
questions.mindset: Purpose is only shared if it survives being compressed and being heard alongside everything else.

questions.stem: A council's library modernisation claims £340,000 a year from reduced counter staffing. Reading a portfolio pack, you notice that the customer-contact programme claims the same £340,000, from the same posts, in the same financial year. Both business cases were approved separately and neither mentions the other. Your sponsor chairs neither portfolio board. The library scheme is four months from its investment decision.

options.text: Speak to the other programme's manager and agree between the two of you how the saving should be split across the two cases.
options.rationale: Two project managers reallocating a benefit between business cases are amending approved documents that neither of them owns. A tidy answer reached informally is still an unauthorised one.

options.text: Raise the duplication in writing with the portfolio office that holds both cases, before the library scheme's investment decision.
options.rationale: The overlap is visible only at portfolio level and correctable only there, and the investment decision is what makes it urgent. Putting it in writing is what makes it somebody's to act on.

options.text: Remove the saving from the library case, since the contact programme claimed it first and is already further ahead in delivery.
options.rationale: Order of approval is not a principle for allocating a benefit, and unilaterally weakening your own case misrepresents it. The real question is which project actually causes the saving.

options.text: Note the overlap in the library case's assumptions and let the investment board draw its own conclusion when it reviews the case.
options.rationale: Burying a material double count in an assumptions list technically discloses it and practically hides it. A board reading one case cannot see what a different portfolio has already claimed.

questions.explanation: A benefit counted twice makes an organisation's collective purpose add up to more than it can possibly deliver, and the error is invisible from inside either project. It can only be resolved by whoever holds both cases, which makes this a routing problem rather than a judgement one. Doing it in writing, and before the next irreversible decision, is what separates disclosure from a passing remark.
questions.mindset: A benefit the organisation cannot bank twice needs raising with whoever can see both claims.

questions.stem: An occupational health provider's team is asked constantly to add features, and every requester argues that theirs serves the product's purpose: getting an employee seen within five working days of referral. Match each request to the reason it sits outside that purpose. One reason is not used.

prompts.text: A dashboard letting employers see aggregate sickness trends across their workforce.
A module replacing the annual clinical audit spreadsheet the clinicians fill in each March.
A reminder chasing employees who have not booked, which the referral portal already sends.

options.text: It serves a different beneficiary from the one the purpose names
options.rationale: The purpose is about how quickly an employee is seen, and this serves the employer's reporting instead. Valuable to somebody is not the same as serving the beneficiary the goal actually names.

options.text: It operates on a cycle far longer than the one the purpose is about
options.rationale: A yearly audit sits outside a five-day referral cycle by an order of magnitude. Work on a different timescale rarely moves a measure defined on this one.

options.text: The need is already met by something the organisation runs today
options.rationale: Building a second version of a reminder that already goes out adds effort and no result. Checking what exists is the cheapest test of whether a request is genuinely new.

options.text: It would cost more than the benefit it returns
options.rationale: Not used. Cost against benefit is how you rank things that do serve the purpose. None of the three above fails on price; each fails on whether it belongs in the list at all.

questions.explanation: Almost any request can be argued to serve a broadly worded purpose, which is why a purpose earns its keep by what it excludes. The useful tests are structural: does it serve the beneficiary the goal names, does it work on the goal's timescale, and is the need already met elsewhere. Applying those before the cost question is what stops prioritisation becoming a ranked queue of things that never belonged in it.
questions.mindset: A purpose is only worth having if something can fail it.

questions.stem: You are eight weeks into a prison education programme. Your sponsor has twice declined to approve a specific objective, preferring the phrase improving learner outcomes, and today tells you privately that a ministerial funding decision is due in October and that a precise target now could be quoted back at him. Three delivery partners are waiting for direction and two have said they cannot plan without it.

options.text: Propose an objective that holds until October, with a named review point at which it will be reset.
options.rationale: The sponsor's constraint is real and temporary, so the statement has to carry an expiry rather than pretend the uncertainty away. A dated review lets partners plan and lets him revisit it without anything breaking.

options.text: Give the partners planning assumptions of your own, clearly labelled as your working assumptions rather than the sponsor's approved objective.
options.rationale: It unblocks the partners and creates a second statement of purpose with no authority behind it. When the real objective lands, everything planned against yours has to be done again.

options.text: Escalate through the programme board, which can require an approved objective for the record regardless of the ministerial decision.
options.rationale: Forcing an objective through governance overrides a sponsor who has explained himself, and a number extracted that way will be defensive. You would win the artefact and lose the relationship.

options.text: Hold the partners at analysis and design until October, and rebaseline the schedule around the date of the funding decision.
options.rationale: It converts a communication problem into four months of deliberate delay. Much of the work does not turn on the precise target, and the partners asked for direction rather than certainty.

questions.explanation: Vagueness in a stated purpose sometimes protects somebody rather than reflecting confusion, and the first useful step is finding out which. Where the reason is real, the answer is a statement with an explicit horizon and a review point: enough for people to plan against, without committing anyone to a number that is not yet theirs to give. A purpose can be provisional so long as it is dated.
questions.mindset: When certainty is not available, commit to a statement with an expiry rather than to no statement at all.

questions.stem: You have just taken on a small product team at an artisan cheese creamery, building a wholesale ordering tool. In your first week you ask four people what the tool is for. The sales lead says fewer phone orders, a developer says accurate stock figures, the owner says winning three new distributors, and the fourth person is not sure. Nothing is written down anywhere. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Adopt the owner's answer, since winning three new distributors is plainly the commercial reason the tool is being funded.
options.rationale: Taking the most senior answer looks decisive and skips the step where the others are reconciled. The sales lead and the developer are describing things the tool has to do, and neither has been ruled in or out.

options.text: Ask each of them to write down their own version, and use the differences as material for the next retrospective.
options.rationale: Collecting the disagreement without resolving it leaves four purposes in writing instead of four in people's heads. A retrospective is also the wrong forum for a question the team cannot settle among themselves.

options.text: Draft one statement that reconciles the four answers you were given, and agree it with the owner and the team.
options.rationale: Four answers and nothing written down is an absence of shared purpose rather than a conflict between rival ones. Drafting a statement and having it agreed is the fastest way to give the team something to work to.

options.text: Start delivery on the points all four answers have in common, and settle the rest once the tool is in use and people can see it.
options.rationale: The overlap between four vague answers is smaller than it looks and will not carry a single real decision. Deferring the question means answering it repeatedly and inconsistently during delivery.

questions.explanation: Where several people give different accounts of what a piece of work is for, the first job is one written statement they all recognise, agreed with whoever owns it. Taking one person's version because of their seniority skips the reconciliation, and gathering the versions without resolving them leaves the team where it started. A purpose that exists only in people's heads is several purposes.
questions.mindset: If nobody can point at the statement, there isn't one yet.

questions.stem: A blood donation service's appointment project is measured against a reduction in donors who book and do not attend. That figure comes from a national reporting extract which the supplier is retiring in three months, and no replacement has been announced. The project runs for another two years and its baseline was taken from that same extract. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Take a final extract before the service is retired and use it as a fixed baseline for the remainder of the two years.
options.rationale: A frozen baseline with nothing to compare it against is half a measure. The difficulty is the absence of future readings, not the loss of the historical ones.

options.text: Change the objective to something measurable from data the service already controls and expects to keep.
options.rationale: It lets the availability of data decide what the project is for. An objective should change because the purpose changed, not because a supplier retired a report.

options.text: Ask the supplier and the national reporting team what will replace the extract, and from what date it will be available.
options.rationale: Three months is enough time to find out whether the gap is real, and the answer determines everything else. Acting on an assumed loss before checking would be premature.

options.text: Raise the measurement gap with the benefits owner now, since it affects how the objective itself can be evidenced.
options.rationale: Whoever owns the benefit needs to know that the evidence for it is about to disappear. Raising it while there is time to arrange an alternative is the difference between a decision and a discovery.

options.text: Continue as planned and take the measurement question to the next annual benefits review, once the position is clearer.
options.rationale: By then the extract will have stopped and the intervening months will be unmeasured. A known expiry three months away is not something an annual cycle can absorb.

questions.explanation: An objective depends on the continued existence of whatever evidences it, and that dependency is rarely written down anywhere. When the evidence is going away, the immediate work is establishing what replaces it and telling whoever owns the benefit while options remain. Redefining the objective to fit the surviving data inverts the relationship — measurement serves the purpose, and letting it choose the purpose is how projects end up aiming at whatever is easy to count.
questions.mindset: Know what evidences the objective, and treat a threat to the evidence as a threat to the objective.
